why_how.text: Looking far enough ahead and keeping space around you buys the reaction time that prevents crashes.
Blind spots hide vehicles that mirrors miss, so a shoulder glance protects every lane change.

reasoning.text: Tailgating compresses reaction time, so widen the gap ahead for the tailgater behind, hold your course, then merge right.

result.text: Ravi lets more space open in front of him, keeps a steady course, and moves right when he can so the tailgater can pass.

correction.text: Blind spots sit beside and slightly behind you, so a shoulder glance that moves only your head is needed before lane changes.

rationale.text: Scanning ten seconds ahead buys reaction time and helps you avoid last-second moves.

narration.text: This lesson is about seeing what is around you and keeping space on every side. The handbook maps the area around your car into zones: green ahead, blue beside, yellow for blind spots, and red behind. We will look at how far ahead to scan, how much following distance to keep, how to handle a tailgater, how to keep room at your sides, and how to check your blind spots. Each of these buys you the most valuable thing a driver can have in an emergency, which is time to react before a problem reaches you. Scan about ten seconds ahead.

Map the zones around your car: green ahead, blue beside, yellow for the blind spots, and red behind. Keep your eyes moving, and scan about ten seconds ahead. Looking that far down the road buys you reaction time and helps you avoid last-second moves, because you see trouble developing before you reach it. A driver who only watches the car directly in front has little warning when something goes wrong farther ahead. So the habit is to keep your eyes moving across all four zones, with your forward scan reaching about ten seconds ahead.

Tailgating blinds you to what is ahead and compresses your reaction time, so hold three seconds behind the vehicle ahead. If someone cuts in front of you, lift off the gas to restore the gap. If someone is tailgating you, widen the gap ahead, hold your course, and then merge right to let them pass. Leave extra room behind motorcycles on metal surfaces and gravel. The three-second rule turns tailgating pressure into gap management: lifting off, holding course, and merging right instead of reacting with sudden moves.

lines.text: Avoid others' blind spots; never pace.

narration.text: Mind your flanks. Stay out of other drivers' blind spots and never pace alongside another vehicle. Open room for freeway mergers even when you hold priority, leave space beside parked cars, and look both ways even when you face a red light or a stop sign. Your own blind spots sit beside and slightly behind you. Check them with a shoulder glance that moves only your head before lane changes, turns, merges, backing, pulling away, parking moves, curb pullouts, and opening your door. That covers both halves: avoid theirs, and check yours.

lines.text: Truth: blind spots need a glance.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Many drivers check the mirrors and move over, assuming the mirrors show everything. They do not. Blind spots sit beside and slightly behind the driver, and the only way to see them is a quick shoulder glance that moves only your head. A second trap is pacing alongside another vehicle for a long stretch. That parks you in someone else's blind spot, so avoid it. A third trap is following closely in heavy traffic; tailgating compresses your reaction time, so hold three seconds and widen the gap when someone tailgates you.

lines.text: How far ahead do you scan?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how far ahead does the handbook say to scan, measured in seconds? Decide first. The answer is about ten seconds ahead. Scanning that far buys reaction time and helps you avoid last-second moves. Keep this number apart from the following gap, which is three seconds behind the vehicle ahead. Ten seconds is how far your eyes reach; three seconds is how much space you keep. If you answered ten, you have the scan rule. If you answered three, you used the following gap, so tie ten to looking and three to spacing.

lines.text: Scan ten seconds; keep three seconds.

narration.text: To wrap up, map the four zones around your car and scan about ten seconds ahead. Hold three seconds behind the vehicle ahead, lift off when someone cuts in, and for a tailgater, widen the gap ahead, hold your course, and merge right. Leave room behind motorcycles on metal and gravel. Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, never pace alongside, make room for freeway mergers, and look both ways even at red lights and stop signs. Check your own blind spots with a head-only shoulder glance before every lane change, turn, merge, backing move, or door opening.

why_how.text: Checking behind you prevents rear-end crashes, and using lights well at night keeps you seeing and seen.

scenario.text: At night on a dark country road, Lu sees a single light coming toward her.

reasoning.text: Single approaching lights may be a bike, a motorcycle, or a car with a dead lamp, so give them a far-right berth.

result.text: Lu slows and moves to the far right until the light has passed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking parking lights are enough in rain.

correction.text: Rain means low beams, never parking lights alone.

memory_support.text: Look back, dim for others, low beams in rain.

prompt.text: If oncoming high beams blind you, where should you look?

answer.text: To the right or off to the side, without retaliating.

rationale.text: When blinded, look right or aside and never flash back.

narration.text: This lesson covers two kinds of awareness: watching behind you, and driving after dark. Rear checks defeat rear-end crashes, so you need to know when to look back. At night, your headlights decide how far ahead you can see, and other people's lights can blind you. We will cover when to check behind, when to use and dim high beams, what to do when oncoming lights blind you, why rain calls for low beams, and the extra care that night walkers, riders, work zones, and single approaching lights demand. These habits keep you seeing and being seen.

lines.text: Sweep mirrors and turn your head.

narration.text: Rear checks defeat rear-end crashes. Sweep your mirrors and turn your head when changing lanes, checking blind spots, slowing down, turning into a driveway, parking, pulling away from a curb, and backing. Each of those moves changes what the drivers behind you need to do, so you check before you make it. A driver who slows suddenly without looking back gives the driver behind no warning. So rear checks mirror your side checks: whenever your move affects traffic behind you, sweep the mirrors and turn your head first, then make the move smoothly.

lines.text: High beams on dark open roads.
Rain: low beams, never parking lights.

narration.text: Use high beams on dark, open roads, and drive so you can stop within the stretch your lights illuminate. Dim them for oncoming traffic. If oncoming lights blind you, look to the right or aside, and do not retaliate by flashing your own lights. When it rains, use low beams, never parking lights alone. High beams trade distance against blinding others: they help you see farther, but only when no one is coming toward you. So high beams on empty dark roads, low beams when others are near, and low beams whenever it rains.

Night walkers, riders, and work zones demand extra care and slower speeds. Your eyes also need time to adjust when you leave a brightly lit place, so give yourself a moment of caution after leaving a lit station or parking lot. A single approaching light may be a bicycle, a motorcycle, or a car with a dead headlight, so give it a far-right berth. Night singles out four concerns: walkers and riders, work zones, the lag while your eyes adjust, and one-light mysteries. Each one calls for slowing down and giving more room.

lines.text: Trap: flash back at bright lights.
Truth: look right, do not retaliate.

narration.text: Here is a trap. When an oncoming driver leaves high beams on, many drivers flash their own high beams in return. The handbook says not to retaliate. Instead, look to the right or aside until the vehicle passes. A second trap is switching to parking lights alone in rain or dusk; rain means low beams, never parking lights alone. A third trap is treating a single light as a car and holding your lane. A single approaching light may be a bike, a motorcycle, or a car with a dead lamp, so move to the far right. Rain means low beams.

Here is a quick check: if oncoming high beams blind you, where should you look? Settle on your answer. The answer is to the right or off to the side, without retaliating. Looking toward the edge of your lane keeps you on course while the bright lights pass. Flashing your own high beams back is not the answer. If you answered look right or aside, you have the rule. Remember the rest of the night picture too: high beams on dark open roads, dim for oncoming traffic, and low beams in rain, never parking lights alone. Look right, never retaliate.

lines.text: Check behind before slowing or turning.
Dim for others; low beams in rain.

narration.text: To wrap up, rear checks defeat rear-end crashes: sweep the mirrors and turn your head when changing lanes, slowing, turning into a driveway, parking, pulling from a curb, or backing. Use high beams on dark open roads, stop within the lit stretch, and dim for oncoming traffic. If blinded, look right or aside without retaliating. In rain, use low beams, never parking lights alone. At night, take extra care and slow down for walkers, riders, and work zones, give your eyes time to adjust after bright places, and give a single approaching light a far-right berth.

why_how.text: Skids happen when tires lose traction, and the right response depends on the surface and your brakes.
Slowing by the right amount for the surface keeps traction before trouble starts.

scenario.text: Jo drives a car with rear-wheel ABS and the rear wheels lock during hard braking.

reasoning.text: Rear ABS calls for easing the pedal until the wheels roll, then steering into the skid.

result.text: Jo eases off the brake until the wheels roll and steers into the skid to regain control.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should brake hard as soon as a skid starts on ice.

correction.text: In a skid, lift off, skip the brakes, steer into it, and look for dry pavement.

memory_support.text: Wet shaves miles, snow halves, ice crawls at five.

prompt.text: On packed snow, how much should you reduce your speed?

rationale.text: Packed snow halves speed, wet roads cut five to ten miles per hour, and ice caps at five.

narration.text: This lesson covers glare and traction. Glare can blind you, and skids happen when your tires lose their grip on the road. We will look at how to fight glare, how to prevent and recover from a skid on slippery surfaces, how to brake out of a locked-wheel skid depending on what kind of brakes your car has, and how much to slow down on wet, snowy, and icy roads. We will also see which parts of the road freeze first. The goal is to keep traction before trouble starts, and to respond calmly if it is lost anyway. Ice caps speed at five.

Fight glare with clean glass, polarized sunglasses, roomy following gaps, and a working sun visor. Watch carefully for pedestrians, who are harder to see in glare, and avoid driving straight into sunrise and sunset when you can. Each of these either cuts the glare itself or gives you more time to react when you cannot see well. Dirty glass scatters light and makes glare worse, so keeping the windshield clean is one of the simplest fixes. When glare hits, leave extra space ahead so a sudden stop does not catch you. Avoid sunrise and sunset runs.

lines.text: In a skid: lift off, steer in.

narration.text: A skid means your tires have lost traction. On ice and snow, skids are worst when you are going fast or downhill. Prevent them by slowing early for curves, avoiding fast turns and sudden stops, shifting to a lower gear before going downhill, and steering around slick patches. If you do skid, lift off the gas, skip the brakes, steer into the skid, and look for dry pavement. Glare fights back with glass, shades, gaps, visors, and timing, while slippery-surface slides are answered by lifting, skipping the brakes, steering in, and hunting for dry pavement.

lines.text: Front ABS: release; no ABS: pump.

narration.text: Locked-wheel skids follow hard, fast braking. How you respond depends on your brakes. With four-wheel ABS, keep firm pressure on the pedal. With rear-wheel ABS, ease off until the wheels roll, then steer into the skid. With front-wheel ABS, release the pedal and straighten the wheel. Without ABS, pump the brakes. If the pedal sinks, pump gently and use downshifts and the emergency brake. Wet brakes can be dried by pressing the gas and brake lightly together. So locked skids are answered by firm, eased, or released pedals, or by pumping.

lines.text: Wet: cut five to ten miles per hour.

narration.text: Slow down by surface. On wet roads, cut five to ten miles per hour. On packed snow, halve your speed. On ice, crawl at no more than five. Shade hides ice that freezes first and dries last, and bridges freeze first. The first rain on dry pavement brings up oil, so slow down immediately when it starts. So slippery roads staircase down by surface: wet shaves a few miles, snow halves, ice crawls at five, with shaded spots and bridges freezing before the rest of the road. Watch for those spots even when the rest of the road looks fine.

lines.text: Trap: brake hard in a slide.
Truth: lift off, skip the brakes.

narration.text: Here is a trap. When a car starts to slide on ice, the instinct is to stand on the brakes. For a slippery-surface skid, the handbook says the opposite: lift off the gas, skip the brakes, steer into the skid, and look for dry pavement. A second trap is pumping the brakes in a car with four-wheel ABS. Pumping is for cars without ABS; four-wheel ABS takes firm pressure. A third trap is assuming a bridge is fine because the road before it was dry. Bridges freeze first, and shaded spots stay icy longest. Lift off and steer in.

Here is a quick check: on packed snow, how much should you reduce your speed? Make your call. The answer is to cut it in half. The other surface rules sit on either side: wet roads cut five to ten miles per hour, and ice caps your speed at five. If you answered half, you have the snow rule. If you mixed it up, picture a staircase going down: wet shaves a few miles off, snow halves your speed, and ice crawls at five. Remember that shade and bridges freeze first, so slow before you reach them. Packed snow halves speed.

lines.text: Skids: lift off, steer in; brake by ABS type.

narration.text: To sum up, fight glare with clean glass, polarized shades, roomy gaps, and a working visor, and avoid sunrise and sunset runs. Prevent skids by slowing early for curves, avoiding fast turns and stops, and downshifting before descents; in a skid, lift off, skip the brakes, steer into it, and look for dry pavement. In a locked-wheel skid, four-wheel ABS takes firm pressure, rear ABS eases then steers, front ABS releases, and cars without ABS pump. Wet roads cut five to ten miles per hour, packed snow halves speed, and ice caps at five, with shade and bridges freezing first.

why_how.text: Bad weather cuts how far you can see and how well you can stop, so the handbook sets clear limits and steps.
Water on the road can float a car or sweep it away.

scenario.text: Kim's car starts to feel light and float on standing water during a heavy rain.

reasoning.text: Hydroplaning floats the car on water with no road contact, so slight inputs can trigger a spin; ease off without touching the brakes.

result.text: Kim eases off the gas, keeps the wheel steady, and does not brake until the tires grip again.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can judge a flooded road's depth by looking.

correction.text: Flood depths are unreadable, so deep water means finding another route.

memory_support.text: Storm thirty, float without braking, flood reroute.

prompt.text: What should you do right after driving through water?

rationale.text: Forced crossings go slowly, and brakes get tested right after leaving the water.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving in bad weather: storms, hydroplaning, getting stuck in snow or mud, floods, high winds, fog and smoke, and the traffic breaks officers use to slow traffic in dangerous conditions. Weather cuts how far you can see and how well your tires grip, so the handbook gives specific limits and steps for each condition. Some of the most important advice is about when not to drive at all, such as postponing trips in heavy fog or rerouting around deep water. We will take each condition in turn and pair the ones that are easy to confuse.

lines.text: Storms: sight near one hundred feet, speed thirty.

narration.text: Storms can cut your sight to about one hundred feet, and then your speed should be no more than thirty. Run your wipers, low beams, and defroster, clear mud and snow off your windows and lights, and carry the correct chains in snow country. Hydroplaning happens when the car floats on water with no road contact, so even slight inputs can trigger a spin. Prevent it with slow speeds, by avoiding standing water, and with gentle lane changes. If the car floats, ease off the gas without touching the brakes until the tires grip again.

lines.text: Gentle gas, rock forward and back.

narration.text: If you get stuck in snow or mud, use a low gear and keep the wheels straight. Press the gas gently so the wheels do not spin. Rock the car forward and back to work it free. Boards or branches under the tires can help, but place them only while the car is stopped. The storm picture then pairs the hundred-foot sight line with the thirty cap plus wipers, lights, defroster, and chains, hydroplaning with brake-free easing, and getting stuck with rocking and traction aids. Each answer is gentle and steady rather than forceful.

lines.text: Deep water: reroute; test brakes after.
Wind: slow, grip, no cruise control.

narration.text: Floods threaten to sweep cars away, hide debris, collapse the road, cause breakdowns, and even electrocute, and you cannot read how deep the water is. Deep water means rerouting. If you must cross, go slowly, and test your brakes right after. High winds threaten tall vehicles most. Slow down, grip the wheel firmly, watch for debris, avoid cruise control, and pull over to wait out the worst. Floods stack five distinct killers behind unreadable depths, with rerouting beating slow crossings, while winds slow tall rigs into firm grips without cruise control.

lines.text: Low beams, stop within sight distance.

narration.text: In fog or smoke, postponing the trip is best. If you must go, drive slowly on low beams, never parking lights, and keep a speed at which you can stop within the distance you can see. Widen gaps, wipe and defog, stay in your lane, listen for traffic you cannot see, and pull off with flashers if it gets too thick. In a traffic break, patrol cars weave across lanes with lights on to slow traffic. Turn on your flashers, match the officer's gentle pace at a distance, and never pass until the lights go off and conditions clear.

Here is a trap. Drivers often look at a flooded road, guess the water is shallow, and drive in. The handbook warns that flood depths are unreadable, and floods can sweep cars away, hide debris, collapse the road, and electrocute. Deep water means rerouting. A second trap is braking when the car starts to hydroplane. Ease off the gas without touching the brakes. A third trap is passing patrol cars during a traffic break to get ahead. Never pass until the lights go off and conditions clear; match the officer's pace instead.

Here is a quick check: what should you do right after driving through water? Choose your answer. The answer is to test your brakes. Water can affect how well the brakes work, so a forced crossing should be slow, and the brakes get tested as soon as you are through. Better still, avoid deep water by finding another route, since you cannot read its depth. If you answered test the brakes, you have the post-water rule. Keep it with the other flood steps: reroute when you can, cross slowly when you must, and test the brakes after.

To sum up, when storms cut sight to about one hundred feet, keep speed at thirty or less with wipers, low beams, and defroster, and carry chains in snow country. If you hydroplane, ease off without braking. If stuck, use a low gear, gentle gas, and rocking, with boards only while stopped. Reroute around deep floods, cross slowly if you must, and test the brakes after. In high winds, slow down, grip firmly, and skip cruise control. In fog, postpone or drive slowly on low beams, and in a traffic break, follow the officer and never pass.

why_how.text: In a crash, unbelted bodies keep flying at travel speed, so belts and the right child seats save lives.

reasoning.text: Children under eight or under four-nine ride restrained in the back seat, except in narrow front-seat cases.

result.text: Ana buckles her niece into an approved child restraint in the back seat.

correction.text: The shoulder strap goes snug across the chest, never under the arm or behind the back.

memory_support.text: Strap on chest, lap on hips, kids by size.

rationale.text: The lap belt sits low on the hips to keep the body from sliding under it.

narration.text: This lesson covers seat belts and child restraints. The belt law binds everyone in the vehicle, and drivers answer for unbelted passengers under sixteen. We will look at why belts matter in a crash, how to wear a belt correctly, including during pregnancy, and the stages a child moves through, from rear-facing seats to standard belts. These rules are about keeping bodies in place during a crash, when everything inside the car keeps moving at the speed you were traveling. Getting the fit right matters as much as buckling up.

Seat belt rules bind everyone, with tickets for those who skip them, and drivers answer for unbelted passengers under sixteen. The reason is crash physics. In a crash, an unbelted body keeps flying at the speed the car was traveling, into the glass or across the seats. A belt holds you in position and softens the blows. Belt law binds riders and drivers alike, crash physics explains the flying body and the sling across seats, and correct wear keeps the straps in the places that protect you. Buckling is the first step; wearing it right is the second.

lines.text: Shoulder strap snug across the chest.
Lap belt low on the hips.

narration.text: Wear the shoulder strap snug across your chest, never under your arm or behind your back. Wear the lap belt low on your hips, which keeps your body from sliding under it in a crash. During pregnancy, route the lap belt low under the belly and the shoulder strap between the breasts and to the side of the bulge. Correct wear routes the straps across the chest and low hips, with the pregnancy routing as the one adjustment. A belt worn under the arm or behind the back cannot hold you in place the way it was designed to.

lines.text: Under eight or four-nine: back seat.

narration.text: Children ride in approved restraints by size. The youngest, under two and under forty pounds, ride rear-facing, and never in front of an airbag. Children under eight, or shorter than four feet nine inches, ride restrained in the back seat, with a few narrow front-seat exceptions. At eight, or four feet nine inches, a child may move to a standard seat belt. Have the installation checked by professionals. So child restraints staircase by size: rear-facing for the youngest, back-seat restraints until eight or four-nine, then standard belts.

lines.text: Truth: across the chest, lap on hips.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Some people tuck the shoulder strap under the arm or behind the back because it feels more comfortable. The handbook says the shoulder strap must sit snug across the chest, never under the arm or behind the back, and the lap belt must sit low on the hips. A second trap is moving a child to a standard seat belt too early. Children ride restrained in the back until they reach eight or four feet nine inches. A third trap is placing a rear-facing seat in front of an airbag, which the handbook forbids. Children under eight ride in back.

lines.text: The lap part of the belt.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: where should the lap part of a seat belt sit? Decide on your answer. The answer is low on the hips. Worn there, it keeps your body from sliding under the belt in a crash. The shoulder strap goes snug across the chest, never under the arm or behind the back. During pregnancy, the lap belt sits low under the belly. If you answered low on the hips, you have the fit rule. If you said across the stomach, remember that the lap belt belongs below the belly, across the hips. Lap belt low on the hips.

lines.text: Everyone buckles; drivers answer for under-sixteens.

narration.text: To wrap up, seat belt rules bind everyone, and drivers answer for unbelted passengers under sixteen. In a crash, an unbelted body keeps flying at travel speed, while a belt holds you in position and softens the blows. Wear the shoulder strap snug across the chest, never under the arm or behind the back, and the lap belt low on the hips; in pregnancy, route the lap belt under the belly. The youngest children ride rear-facing and never in front of an airbag, children under eight or four feet nine inches ride restrained in the back, and installs should be checked by professionals.

why_how.text: Sitting too close to an airbag or leaving a child in a hot car can be deadly, and safe speed depends on conditions, not just signs.

scenario.text: It is a rainy evening and Max is on a highway where no lower limit is posted.

reasoning.text: The Basic Speed Law bans speeds unsafe for conditions regardless of signs, and the highway default is sixty-five.

result.text: Max drives below sixty-five because the rain and traffic make that speed unsafe.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a posted or default limit is always a safe speed.

correction.text: The Basic Speed Law bans any speed unsafe for conditions, whatever the signs say.

memory_support.text: Ten inches back, never alone, safe for conditions.

prompt.text: What is the default speed limit on a two-lane road?

rationale.text: The defaults are sixty-five on highways and fifty-five on two-lane roads and while towing.

narration.text: This lesson brings together three safety rules. Airbags work with seat belts, but sitting too close to one can hurt you. Children and animals must never be left in hot parked cars, and young children must never be left alone in a car. And the Basic Speed Law sets the rule behind every speed limit: drive at a speed that is safe for conditions. We will look at the airbag distance, the age rules for leaving a child in a car, why heat in a parked car is so dangerous, and the default speed limits that apply when no other limit is posted.

lines.text: Sit ten inches from the cover.
Children near side bags at risk.

narration.text: Airbags assist seat belts; they do not replace them. Drivers and passengers should sit at least ten inches from the airbag cover, measured from the chest to the steering wheel. Drivers who find that hard to manage can get advice from a dealer. Children seated beside side airbags face serious risk. So the airbag rule is a distance: ten inches between your chest and the cover, for every seat with an airbag. Moving your seat back and adjusting the wheel helps you reach that distance while still controlling the car comfortably.

lines.text: Supervisor must be twelve or older.
Heat spikes even with cracked windows.

narration.text: Never leave a child aged six or younger alone in a car; a supervisor aged twelve or older is required. Never leave children or animals in a hot parked car. Heat inside a parked car spikes quickly, even with the windows cracked, and can lead to dehydration, heatstroke, and death. So two rules protect children in cars: the supervision rule for those six and under, and the hot-car rule for children and animals of any age. A cracked window does not make a hot car safe, and a short errand does not change either rule. Supervisors must be twelve or older.

The Basic Speed Law bans speeds that are unsafe for conditions, regardless of what the signs say. It weighs traffic, road surfaces, pedestrians, weather, and congestion, and it does not allow weaving on freeways. The default limits are sixty-five on highways and fifty-five on two-lane roads and while towing. So the default limit is the most you may drive when conditions are good, not a speed you must keep. In rain, heavy traffic, or poor visibility, the Basic Speed Law requires you to slow down below the default to a speed that is safe.

lines.text: Trap: the limit is always safe.
Truth: safe for conditions comes first.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Drivers often think that driving at the posted or default limit is always legal. The Basic Speed Law bans speeds unsafe for conditions regardless of the signs, so sixty-five on a highway in heavy rain can still break the law. A second trap is leaving a young child in the car for a quick errand. Children six and under must not be left alone; a supervisor twelve or older is required. A third trap is cracking a window and assuming the car will stay cool. Heat still spikes and can cause heatstroke and death.

Here is a quick check: what is the default speed limit on a two-lane road? Make your choice. The answer is fifty-five, which is also the default while towing. On highways, the default is sixty-five. Remember that these defaults are the most you may drive in good conditions; the Basic Speed Law still bans any speed that is unsafe for traffic, surfaces, pedestrians, weather, or congestion. If you answered fifty-five, you have the two-lane default. If you answered sixty-five, you used the highway number, so tie fifty-five to two-lane roads and towing.

To sum up, airbags assist seat belts, and drivers and passengers should sit at least ten inches from the cover, measured from chest to wheel, with dealers advising drivers who struggle to manage it. Children beside side airbags face serious risk. Never leave a child six or younger alone in a car without a supervisor twelve or older, and never leave children or animals in a hot parked car, where heat spikes even with cracked windows. The Basic Speed Law bans speeds unsafe for conditions, with defaults of sixty-five on highways and fifty-five on two-lane roads and while towing.

why_how.text: Calm, practiced responses to blowouts, pavement drops and breakdowns keep a bad moment from becoming a crash.
Free freeway patrol help is reached by calling five-eleven.

scenario.text: Sam's front tire blows out at freeway speed.

reasoning.text: A blowout forbids panic braking or lifting: grip with both hands, hold speed while safe, ease off the gas, steer straight, then slow and pull off.

result.text: Sam grips the wheel, keeps the car straight, eases off the gas, and slows gradually before pulling off the road.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should yank the wheel to get back on the pavement fast.

correction.text: After leaving the pavement, grip firmly, ease off the gas, brake gently, check behind, and reenter carefully, never with a violent yank.

prompt.text: What phone number do you call for freeway patrol help?

rationale.text: Freeway patrols give free help during commute hours, reached through five-eleven.

narration.text: This lesson covers emergencies on the road and how to handle them calmly. We will look at what to do when two hazards appear at once, how to handle a tire blowout, how to get back onto the road after your wheels leave the pavement, what heat waves and cold snaps mean for your car, what to do if your car fails on the freeway, and the free help freeway patrols can give. The common thread is control: avoid panic inputs like hard braking or sudden yanks, keep a firm grip, and make each move smoothly and in order. Grip the wheel with both hands.

lines.text: Handle the more severe danger first.
Bike plus oncoming car: slow, yield, pass.

narration.text: When two dangers appear together, split them by severity and handle the more serious one first. For example, if a bicyclist is ahead and a car is coming toward you, slow down, let the oncoming car pass, and then pass the bicyclist with three feet of space, or use the left lane when traffic flows steadily. Trying to deal with both at once is what leads to squeezing a rider against oncoming traffic. Dual hazards resolve by severity, with the bike getting three feet after the oncoming traffic clears, one hazard at a time.

lines.text: Grip, hold, ease off, steer straight.

narration.text: In a blowout, do not brake in a panic or lift off suddenly. Grip the wheel with both hands, hold your speed while it is safe, ease off the gas, steer straight to stabilize the car, look where you want to go, and then slow down and pull off. If your wheels leave the pavement, keep a firm grip, take your foot off the gas, brake gently, check behind you, and reenter carefully. Never yank the wheel violently back toward oncoming traffic. Blowouts and drop-offs share one lesson: steady hands and gentle inputs keep control.

lines.text: Heat: gauges, no speeding, AC off.

narration.text: In heat waves, watch your gauges, avoid sustained speeding, and turn the air conditioning off. In cold snaps, watch the gauges for antifreeze gaps and defrost or crack the windows; your owner's manual holds the details. If your car fails on the freeway, pull fully to the right, exiting and reentering from the right, call five-eleven or find a call box, return to your car quickly, and stay belted inside with flashers on as needed. Leave the car only when there is no shoulder or guardrail, or a true refuge is close by.

During commute hours, freeway patrols give free help: a few gallons of gas, jump starts, radiator patches, flat tire changes, crash reports, and free tows to approved spots when the car will not run. They do not provide private tows, shop recommendations, help for motorcycles, or crash help unless directed. You reach them through five-eleven. So freeway failures pull right with right-side exits, five-eleven calls, belted waiting, and rare abandonment, and the patrols cover gas, jumps, patches, flats, reports, and tows, minus private tows, tips, motorcycles, and crashes.

lines.text: Trap: brake hard after a blowout.

narration.text: Here is a trap. When a tire blows out, the instinct is to slam the brakes. The handbook forbids panic braking or lifting off suddenly. Grip with both hands, hold your speed while it is safe, ease off the gas, and steer straight. A second trap is yanking the wheel to get back onto the pavement after your wheels drop off. Never make violent yanks toward oncoming traffic; brake gently, check behind, and reenter carefully. A third trap is leaving a broken-down car to walk on the freeway. Stay belted inside unless there is no shoulder or a true refuge.

lines.text: Your car fails on the freeway.

While you wait, pull fully right, stay belted inside, and use flashers as needed. If you answered five-eleven, you have the breakdown call. Keep it with the rest of the breakdown routine.

lines.text: Steady hands; pull right; call five-eleven.

narration.text: To wrap up, handle the more severe of two hazards first, passing a bike with three feet once oncoming traffic clears. In a blowout, avoid panic braking, grip with both hands, hold speed while safe, ease off, steer straight, then slow and pull off. After leaving the pavement, reenter gently, never with a violent yank. In heat, watch gauges, avoid sustained speeding, and turn off the air conditioning; in cold, watch antifreeze and defrost. On a freeway breakdown, pull fully right, call five-eleven, stay belted inside, and use free patrol help.

why_how.text: Knowing exactly how to escape a car stuck on tracks, and keeping your attention on the road, can save your life.

scenario.text: Lia's car stalls on a railroad crossing; the lights start flashing and a train is coming.

reasoning.text: With a train coming and flashers on, exit instantly, run diagonally away toward the side the train is coming from, then call emergency services.

result.text: Lia gets out at once, runs diagonally toward the train's side away from the tracks, and then calls for help.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking hands-free phone use is allowed for teen drivers.

correction.text: Minors face a total wireless ban behind the wheel, except emergency calls.

memory_support.text: Train coming: run toward it diagonally. No train: call the posted number.

prompt.text: Stuck on tracks with no train in sight and no flashers, what number do you call first?

answer.text: The posted crossing number, giving the crossing ID.

rationale.text: With no train or flashers, get out, call the posted number with the crossing ID, then call emergency services.

narration.text: This lesson covers four dangers: being stuck on railroad tracks, distraction from phones and other sources, the unusual behavior of driver assistance systems and self-driving vehicles, and carbon monoxide. Each one has a clear rule. The track escape depends on whether a train is coming. Phone rules differ for adults and minors. Assistance systems can react in ways a human would not. And carbon monoxide gives no smell, so you must know its warning signs. We will take each in turn, starting with what to do if your car is trapped on the tracks.

lines.text: Train and flashers: get out, run diagonally.
No train: call the posted number.

narration.text: If your car is trapped on the tracks and a train is coming with the lights flashing, get out immediately and run diagonally away from the tracks, toward the side the train is coming from, then call emergency services. If there is no train and no flashing lights, get out, call the posted crossing number and give the crossing ID so the car can be reported, then call emergency services. Track entrapment splits on train presence: flashers mean an instant exit and a diagonal run toward the train's side, while no train means calling the posted number first.

Distraction kills, whether it comes from phones, navigation, children, pets, music, or grooming. Holding a phone while driving is illegal. Adults may use a phone hands-free, and only when needed. Let calls go to voicemail or pull over, and let texts and emails wait every time. A phone may be mounted on the windshield, dashboard, or console where it does not block your view, and used with a single swipe only. Minors face a total ban on wireless devices behind the wheel, except for emergency calls. So adults go hands-free only when needed, and minors not at all.

Driver assistance systems and self-driving vehicles react in ways a human driver would not, so expect unusual responses to road events from them. Carbon monoxide comes from exhaust pipes and kills without any smell, so never let an engine idle in a closed garage. Tiredness, yawning, dizziness, nausea, headaches, and ringing in the ears are all warning signs that call for an exhaust check. So the phone rules pair mounted single-swipe use for adults with a total ban for minors, assistance systems warn of unusual reactions, and carbon monoxide pairs the garage ban with a symptom watchlist.

lines.text: Trap: run straight down the tracks.
Truth: run diagonally toward the train's side.

narration.text: Here is a trap. People stuck on tracks with a train coming often run straight along the tracks or away from the train. The handbook says to run diagonally away from the tracks toward the side the train is coming from, and only then call emergency services, once you are clear of the tracks and away from the car. A second trap is staying in the car to try to restart it when a train is coming; exit instantly. A third trap is thinking a teen may use a hands-free phone; minors face a total wireless ban except emergency calls.

Here is a quick check: your car is stuck on the tracks, with no train in sight and no flashing lights. What number do you call first? Decide first. The answer is the posted crossing number, giving the crossing ID, so the car can be reported. Then call emergency services. If a train were coming with the lights flashing, the order would change: get out instantly, run diagonally toward the train's side, and call emergency services afterward. If you answered the posted number, you have the no-train rule and the split between the two cases.

lines.text: No handhelds; watch for carbon monoxide.

narration.text: To finish this section, if your car is trapped on the tracks with a train coming and lights flashing, get out, run diagonally toward the train's side, and call emergency services. With no train, get out, call the posted crossing number with the crossing ID, then call emergency services. Holding a phone while driving is illegal, adults go hands-free only when needed, texts always wait, and minors face a total wireless ban except emergencies. Expect unusual reactions from assistance systems, never idle in a closed garage, and check the exhaust if carbon monoxide symptoms appear.
